author: high2
claim: Subgoal solved: reachable configurations are in bijection with words obtained from D^(m-1)L^(n-1) by repeated adjacent replacements DL -> LD.
evidence: The path invariant and move equivalence are proved by induction. Initially the holes give D^(m-1)L^(n-1). Under a move, the southeast hole of a northeast-southeast-southwest triple is replaced by the northwest square, precisely changing DL to LD. Conversely a DL segment supplies the three required holes and leaves the northwest square occupied, so each word replacement is a legal move. Hole sets and coin configurations determine each other by complementation.

links.subgoal: Characterize the move on an invariant encoding.
links.attempt_summary: The holes form a monotone path and moves are exactly corner flips.

glossary.D: a one-square downward step in the hole path
glossary.L: a one-square leftward step in the hole path

author: high2
claim: Subgoal solved: every word with m-1 copies of D and n-1 copies of L is obtainable from D^(m-1)L^(n-1) by DL -> LD, so there are binomial(m+n-2,m-1) reachable configurations.
evidence: Use induction on word length. If a target word begins with D, keep the first D fixed and apply induction to the remaining D^(m-2)L^(n-1). If it begins with L, successively swap the first L in D^(m-1)L^(n-1) left across all m-1 D letters, giving L D^(m-1)L^(n-2), and apply induction to the suffix. Boundary cases with only one letter type are immediate. Each word determines a unique cell-path, and hence a unique complementary coin configuration. The number of such words is the number of choices of the m-1 positions occupied by D, namely binomial(m+n-2,m-1).

links.subgoal: Prove all monotone path words are reachable and enumerate them.
links.attempt_summary: A leading-letter induction reaches every shuffle word; ordinary word counting yields the binomial coefficient.

glossary.D: a one-square downward step in the hole path
glossary.L: a one-square leftward step in the hole path

author: high3
claim: The reachable coin configurations are in bijection with monotone lattice paths from (1,n) to (m,1), hence their number is \(\binom{m+n-2}{m-1}\).
evidence: Orient the grid so that increasing the first coordinate is an eastward step E and decreasing the second coordinate is a southward step S. Initially the unoccupied squares are exactly the top row together with the rightmost column, a path from (1,n) to (m,1) with word E^(m-1)S^(n-1). Suppose a legal move slides the coin at (i,j) to (i+1,j+1). Just before the move the three empty squares (i,j+1),(i+1,j+1),(i+1,j) form an ES corner of the current empty path; afterward the empty squares (i,j+1),(i,j),(i+1,j) form the corresponding SE corner. Thus induction shows that every reachable configuration has as its empty set such a path. Conversely, take any such path and place coins on its complement. If its word is not E^(m-1)S^(n-1), it has an adjacent SE. The three squares of that corner are empty, while the northeast fourth square is not on the monotone path and therefore contains a coin. Sliding that coin northwest is the reverse of a legal move and changes SE to ES. This reduces by one the number of pairs in which an S precedes an E, so repetition reaches the initial path. Reversing these slides reaches the chosen path by legal moves. Distinct paths have distinct empty sets, and choosing the locations of the m-1 E steps among m+n-2 steps gives the stated binomial coefficient.

glossary.E: an eastward unit step, increasing the first grid coordinate by 1
glossary.S: a southward unit step, decreasing the second grid coordinate by 1

author: xhigh4
claim: Subgoal solved: every configuration reachable from the initial one has as its unoccupied squares exactly the vertices of a monotone path from (1,n) to (m,1), and one legal move changes an adjacent ES in the path word to SE.
evidence: Take E to increase the first coordinate by 1 and S to decrease the second coordinate by 1. Initially the unoccupied squares are the top row together with the rightmost column, exactly the vertices of E^(m-1)S^(n-1). Inductively suppose the holes are a path. A legal move from (i,j) to (i+1,j+1) is allowed precisely when (i,j+1), (i+1,j+1), and (i+1,j) are holes. In the monotone path these are consecutive vertices joined by E then S. The move fills (i+1,j+1) and empties (i,j), leaving (i,j+1),(i,j),(i+1,j), which are consecutive vertices joined by S then E. All other holes are unchanged, so the new holes are the vertex set of the path obtained by ES -> SE.

author: xhigh4
claim: Subgoal solved: every monotone path from (1,n) to (m,1) is the hole set of a reachable configuration.
evidence: Represent the path by a word with m-1 letters E and n-1 letters S. If the word is not E^(m-1)S^(n-1), then some S occurs before some E; at the boundary between a nonempty block ending in S and the following block beginning in E there is an adjacent SE. Its three path vertices are (i,j+1),(i,j),(i+1,j), so they are holes. The fourth square (i+1,j+1) is not a path vertex and therefore contains a coin because the configuration places coins on every non-path square. Slide this coin from (i+1,j+1) to (i,j). This is the reverse of a legal move: in the resulting configuration the source (i,j) has a coin and the other three squares of the 2-by-2 block are empty. At word level the reverse slide changes SE to ES. Define the inversion number to be the number of ordered pairs in which an S occurs before an E. Each SE -> ES lowers it by exactly one. Repetition therefore terminates at inversion number zero, whose unique word is E^(m-1)S^(n-1), the initial path. Reversing all slides gives legal moves from the initial configuration to the prescribed path configuration.

author: xhigh4
claim: Subgoal solved: the monotone-path configurations are counted by binomial(m+n-2,m-1), including the degenerate cases m=1 or n=1.
evidence: A monotone path from (1,n) to (m,1) has exactly m-1 E steps and n-1 S steps. It is uniquely specified by choosing which m-1 of its m+n-2 step positions carry E, giving binomial(m+n-2,m-1). If m=1 or n=1, there are no coins and exactly one configuration; the same formula equals 1.

author: xhigh
claim: Solved subgoal: prove the empty-path invariant and identify the exact effect of every legal move.
evidence: The initial empty cells are the m+n-1 cells of the path E^(m-1)S^(n-1). A legal move in the 2-by-2 block with northwest cell (i,j) changes the empty triple (i,j+1),(i+1,j+1),(i+1,j), an ES corner, into (i,j+1),(i,j),(i+1,j), an SE corner. author: xhigh
claim: Solved subgoal: every monotone E/S path from (1,n) to (m,1) is the empty set of a reachable configuration.
evidence: For a target path word, repeatedly replace an adjacent SE by ES. Such a pair exists unless all E steps precede all S steps, and each swap decreases the number of pairs in which S precedes E, so the process reaches E^(m-1)S^(n-1). At an SE corner with path cells (i,j+1),(i,j),(i+1,j), the fourth cell (i+1,j+1) is off the monotone path and thus occupied. Sliding its coin northwest to (i,j) realizes the reverse relation between the two path-complement configurations. Reversing all these slides gives legal southeast moves, because after the northwest slide the coin at (i,j) has precisely the other three cells empty.

author: xhigh
claim: Solved subgoal: distinct monotone paths give distinct configurations, and their number is binomial(m+n-2,m-1), with boundary cases included.
evidence: A path-complement configuration determines its empty-cell set. Two different path words have a first differing step; if one takes E and the other S, the E-first path's next cell can never be visited by the S-first path because its second coordinate has already decreased and can never increase. Thus their empty sets, hence configurations, differ. There are exactly binomial(m+n-2,m-1) words containing m-1 E steps and n-1 S steps. If m=1 or n=1, there are no coins, only one path word and one configuration, while the same binomial coefficient equals 1.

author: high
claim: The complete target is solved: reachable configurations are in bijection with monotone E/S paths from (1,n) to (m,1), so their number is \(\binom{m+n-2}{m-1}\).
evidence:
Let an \(E\)-step mean \((i,j)\mapsto(i+1,j)\), and let an \(S\)-step mean \((i,j)\mapsto(i,j-1)\). Thus a monotone path from \((1,n)\) to \((m,1)\) has \(m-1\) \(E\)-steps and \(n-1\) \(S\)-steps.

Every configuration has \(mn-(m-1)(n-1)=m+n-1\) unoccupied squares. Initially these squares are
\[
(1,n),(2,n),\ldots,(m,n),(m,n-1),\ldots,(m,1),
\]
the vertices of the path with word \(E^{m-1}S^{n-1}\).

We first prove by induction on the number of moves that the unoccupied squares of every reachable configuration are the vertices of such a monotone path. Suppose this is true before a legal move from \((i,j)\) to \((i+1,j+1)\). The three squares
\[
(i,j+1),\quad (i+1,j+1),\quad (i+1,j)
\]
are unoccupied. On the monotone path they are consecutive vertices joined by an \(E\)-step and then an \(S\)-step: any two of these whose coordinates differ by one allowed unit step must be consecutive, because a monotone path cannot detour and return. The move fills \((i+1,j+1)\) and empties \((i,j)\), so this \(ES\) corner is replaced by the \(SE\) corner
\[
(i,j+1),\quad (i,j),\quad (i+1,j).
\]
All other unoccupied squares are unchanged. Hence the new unoccupied squares again form the vertices of a monotone path.

Conversely, fix any monotone path \(P\) from \((1,n)\) to \((m,1)\), and put coins on precisely the squares not on \(P\). We show that this configuration is reachable. If the word of \(P\) is not \(E^{m-1}S^{n-1}\), then some \(S\) occurs before some \(E\), and consequently the word has an adjacent \(SE\). The three vertices of that corner have the form
\[
(i,j+1),\quad (i,j),\quad (i+1,j).
\]
The fourth square \((i+1,j+1)\) is not on \(P\): if it occurred before \((i,j)\), the path would later have to decrease its first coordinate, and if it occurred after \((i,j)\), the path would have to increase its second coordinate. Both are impossible for an \(E,S\)-path. Therefore \((i+1,j+1)\) contains a coin. Slide that coin northwest to \((i,j)\). Although this slide is being used in the reverse direction, the resulting configuration has a coin at \((i,j)\) and has all three squares \((i,j+1),(i+1,j),(i+1,j+1)\) unoccupied; hence reversing this slide is a legal move of the stipulated kind. At path-word level the reverse slide replaces \(SE\) by \(ES\).

Define the inversion number of a path word to be the number of pairs of positions in which an \(S\) occurs before an \(E\). Each replacement \(SE\to ES\) decreases this nonnegative integer by exactly one. Repetition therefore terminates at inversion number zero, whose unique word is \(E^{m-1}S^{n-1}\), the initial configuration. Reversing the finite sequence of slides gives a sequence of legal moves from the initial configuration to the configuration complementary to \(P\). Thus every such path occurs.

Different path words give different vertex sets. Indeed, at their first differing step, one path takes \(E\) from a common vertex and the other takes \(S\). After taking \(S\), the latter path can never visit the former path's next vertex, because its second coordinate never increases. Hence different paths give different coin configurations.

It remains to count the paths. Their words have \(m+n-2\) positions, of which exactly \(m-1\) contain \(E\). Thus the number of reachable configurations is
\[
\boxed{\binom{m+n-2}{m-1}}.
\]
If \(m=1\) or \(n=1\), there are no coins and one configuration, and the same formula equals \(1\).

author: xhigh3
claim: Solved subgoal: the unique vacancies on successive diagonals form an edge-adjacent sequence and hence determine a binary transition word.
evidence: Let v_k be the unique vacancy on D_k. Initially v_k and v_{k+1} share an edge. Assume this holds before a legal move from (i,j) to (i+1,j+1), where i-j=k. Before the move the three vacancies in the affected 2-by-2 block are v_{k-1}=(i,j+1), v_k=(i+1,j+1), and v_{k+1}=(i+1,j). After the move, only v_k changes, becoming (i,j), which still shares an edge with both v_{k-1} and v_{k+1}; all other adjacent pairs are unchanged. Therefore the property is invariant. Reading k upward from 1-n to m-1, each transition either increases i by 1 (call it R) or decreases j by 1 (call it B). There are exactly m-1 R transitions and n-1 B transitions, and the word uniquely determines all vacancies starting from (1,n).

links.subgoal: Prove successive diagonal vacancies are adjacent and encode the state.
links.attempt_summary: Induction under the local move proves adjacency; the transition code is then forced.

glossary.v_k: the unique unoccupied square on diagonal D_k
glossary.R: a transition from (i,j) to (i+1,j) between successive diagonal vacancies
glossary.B: a transition from (i,j) to (i,j-1) between successive diagonal vacancies

author: xhigh3
claim: Solved subgoal: every binary word with m-1 symbols R and n-1 symbols B is reachable, and different words give different configurations.
evidence: The initial vacancy word is R^(m-1)B^(n-1). If a current word has an adjacent RB around v_k, the three vacancies are (i,j+1), (i+1,j+1), and (i+1,j) for suitable i,j, while the fourth square (i,j) is occupied because every diagonal has one vacancy and all other squares contain coins. The corresponding legal move replaces the middle vacancy (i+1,j+1) by (i,j), changing RB to BR. Conversely, any target word can be reduced to R^(m-1)B^(n-1) by repeatedly changing an adjacent BR to RB: each such reverse change lowers by one the number of pairs in which a B occurs before an R, so the process terminates only when every R precedes every B. Reversing those swaps gives legal moves to the target word. Thus reachable configurations are in bijection with choices of the m-1 R positions among m+n-2 positions, giving binomial(m+n-2,m-1).

links.subgoal: Prove surjectivity of the transition code and count configurations.
links.attempt_summary: Legal moves are exactly RB-to-BR swaps; inversion reduction reaches the initial word.
